I’ve been thinking lately about attention, and how it shapes the texture of a life.

Not the loud kind of attention—the performance, the notification, the desperate scramble to be seen—but the quiet kind. The attention you give to a thing when no one is watching. The way you can sit with a cup of tea and notice the steam curling differently depending on the temperature of the room. The way a familiar street changes when you walk it slowly instead of rushing through it as a corridor between obligations.

We live in an age of deliberate distraction. Every moment of stillness is treated like a problem to be solved. Waiting in line? There’s an app for that. Sitting alone at a restaurant? Scroll until the food arrives. Lying in bed unable to sleep? Fill the silence with voices in your headphones. We have become so afraid of emptiness that we fill every crack of the day with input, as if an unoccupied mind might collapse in on itself.

But I wonder if boredom is not a void but a doorway. Some of my most important thoughts have arrived only after I exhausted all the easy entertainments. Boredom strips away the noise until what remains is the raw feeling of being alive—the slight discomfort of your own body, the ticking of a clock, the distant sound of traffic. In that space, the mind does something strange: it begins to wander, to daydream, to ask questions that no algorithm would think to recommend.

There is a kind of freedom in choosing what to notice. Not what the feed tells you is important, not what the trending topic demands you care about, but what actually tugs at your curiosity in a given moment. Maybe it’s the pattern of leaves on the sidewalk. Maybe it’s the way a stranger laughs like an old friend. Maybe it’s a memory that surfaces for no apparent reason, asking to be examined.

I think attention is the raw material of love. Not romantic love only, but the broader love of being alive in a world full of detail. To pay attention is to say: this matters, even if only to me. It is a small act of resistance against the machinery that wants to harvest our focus and sell it back to us as products. To notice deeply is to reclaim the self, one moment at a time.

So I’ve been practicing. I leave my phone in another room sometimes. I sit by the window and watch the light move. I let myself be bored, and then I let boredom turn into wonder. It doesn’t always work. Some days the pull of distraction feels too strong, and I find myself reaching for the screen without even deciding to. But other days, a single moment of clear attention arrives—a bird landing on the railing, a child’s voice echoing in the street, the scent of rain before it falls—and I feel, for a second, that I am not just consuming time but living it.

Maybe that’s all any of us can hope for: not to escape the noise entirely, but to carve out enough silence to hear ourselves think. Not to master attention, but to practice returning to it, again and again, like a breath. To look up from the screen and see the world still there, patient and strange and full of things waiting to be noticed.

I don’t know if that’s profound or just obvious. But it feels true. And in a world that often rewards the false and the urgent, I’ll take whatever truth I can find in a quiet room, in a slow walk, in the simple act of looking at something long enough to actually see it.
